::: {custom-style="Abstract Title"}
Abstract (180 words)
:::

::: {custom-style="Abstract"}

Prognostic models are essential for providing individual survival predictions. We investigate the uncertainty of survival predictions from the Cox proportional hazards model using the concept of effective sample size ($N_{*}$). Effective sample size translates prediction variance into a number of 'patients like you' that a prediction is effectively based on. Properties of $N_{*}$ were investigated in a real-world example of colon cancer patients. Simulation studies clarified the behavior of variance components stemming from baseline hazard and coefficient estimation. Effective sample size can exceed the development sample size ($N_{*} > N$). While this is unintuitive, it does reflect genuine prediction certainty. Still, for communication of uncertainty with patients, we recommend against communicating $N_{*} > N$. Using $N_{*}$ only for the communication of survival predictions between 1% and 90% $(0.01 < S\left( t \middle| x \right) < 0.9$) avoids this. Additionally, $N_{*}$ may be a valuable diagnostic tool for the investigation of individual uncertainty during model development to guard against modeling covariate profiles with high uncertainty. In conclusion, the complex properties of Cox model variance mean that while $N_{*}$ is a valid indicator of uncertainty, its use in patient communication is not always appropriate.
:::

## 1 Introduction

Prognostic models with survival outcomes are widespread in clinical domains such as oncology and cardiology. Examples are the Melanoma Institute Australia models which provide survival predictions for patients at different stages of melanoma,[@pires2022; @varey2024] the PREDICT model for breast cancer treatment decision support,[@predict] and the QRISK3 algorithm predicting the 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease.[@qrisk] Effective implementation and presentation of personalized prognoses supports shared decision-making by addressing the informational needs of both patients and clinicians.[@vromans2021; @4Dpicture]

Uncertainty is an important element of predictions from prognostic models.[@riley2025] Uncertainty in predictions has been used as an argument for and against shared decision-making.[@pieterse2026] Many risk calculators make no mention of prediction uncertainty,[@pires2022; @qrisk] while some show 95% confidence intervals around predicted survival probabilities[@varey2024] or treatment benefit.[@predict] Guidelines such as the TRIPOD+AI[@tripod-ai] statement advise developers to consider sample size requirements to ensure a minimum level of prediction certainty. More recently, focus has shifted to the stability of models and the uncertainty in individual predictions.[@riley2025; @altman1989; @shen2016; @riley2023; @riley2023b; @barrenada2025]

Effective sample size has been suggested as a promising summary measure of individual uncertainty in generalized linear models and machine learning models.[@thomassen2024; @thomassen2025] Effective sample size for a patient's prediction translates the prediction variance to the number of patients with the same covariate values that the prediction was effectively based on. In survival analysis, the concept provides a readily interpretable measure for Kaplan-Meier curves, where it is based on the local information available within the risk set.[@kaplanmeier1958; @hackmann2025; @nemes2026] Extending this concept to survival predictions based on multiple prognostic factors using the Cox proportional hazards model presents a new challenge.

We hypothesize that effective sample size can be used to express uncertainty for multivariable individual survival predictions. To investigate if this measure is useful in clinical practice, we studied two desired properties:

1.  Intuitive behavior: Effective sample size reflects the variance of a sample with complete follow-up, and should preferably not exceed the total sample size. Intuitive behavior is most important in using effective sample size for communicating prediction uncertainty to end users.

2.  Reflection of exceptionality: Effective sample size reflects the exceptionality of a patient profile. This property is most important in using effective sample size as a diagnostic to investigate the distribution of prediction uncertainty in a relevant data sample, e.g. training or validation data.

This paper describes the calculation of effective sample size for the Cox model (Section 2), applies it to real-world data (Section 3), and uses simulations to explore its behavior in depth (Section 4). In the discussion (Section 5), the effective sample size is interpreted with respect to the statistical properties of the Cox model, and potential applications in model development and risk communication are considered.

## 2 Effective sample size for the Cox model

### 2.1 Effective sample size

We consider the Cox proportional hazards model, a semi-parametric survival model in which the hazard function is defined as $h\left( t|x \right) = h_{0}(t)\exp\left( \beta^{\top}x \right)$, with cumulative hazard $H\left( t|x \right) = \int_{0}^{t}h\left( u|x \right) = H_{0}(t)\exp\left( \beta^{\top}x \right)$.[@cox1972]

Suppose we observe $N$ independent individuals with data $(T_{i},Y_{i},x_{i}),$ with $i = 1,\ldots,N,$ where $T_{i}$ is the observed time and $Y_{i} \in \{ 0,1\}$ is the event indicator (1 = event, 0 = censored). Let $t_{1} < \ldots < t_{l}$ denote the distinct ordered event times, and let $d_{j}$ be the number of events occurring at time $t_{j}$. For each event time $t_{j}$, define the risk set $R_{j} = R\left( t_{j} \right) = \{ i:T_{i} \geq t_{j}\}$.

Suppose that we have fitted a Cox proportional hazards model on $(T_{i},Y_{i},x_{i}),$ with $i = 1,\ldots,N,$ yielding estimated cumulative baseline hazard ${\widehat{H}}_{0}(t)$ and estimated coefficient vector $\widehat{\beta} = \left( {\widehat{\beta}}_{1},\ldots,{\widehat{\beta}}_{p} \right)$. The personalized survival prediction for a new patient at a predetermined time $t$ using this Cox model is ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) = \widehat{S}\left( t|x_{\text{new}} \right) = exp\left( - {\widehat{H}}_{0}(t)\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{\text{new}} \right) \right)$, based on their covariate values $x_{\text{new}} = \left( x_{1},\ldots,x_{p} \right)$ .

To define the effective sample size for this patient at time $t$, we take as a reference the situation where we have a number $N_{*}$ patients with identically distributed outcomes who all have the same covariate values $x_{\text{new}}$ as the new patient and are followed from time 0 to $t$ without loss to follow-up. Suppose we would have obtained in this virtual sample the same survival estimate ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) =$ ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$ for the binary outcome survived until time t, yes/no. Then the binomial sampling variance could be estimated by $V_{\text{Bin}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right) = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right)}{N_{*}}$. To calculate effective sample size, we equate the variance of the Cox model prediction ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$ with the binomial sampling variance of the sample mean outcome ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)$:

$$V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right) = V_{\text{Bin}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t) \right)\ \quad(1)$$

We can calculate the number $N_{*}$ as the number of patients required to obtain the same uncertainty in our estimate of ${\widehat{S}}_{N_{*}}(t)$, as in the model estimate of ${\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)$. This number $N_{*}$ is the effective sample size. We can estimate $N_{*}$ using:

$$N_{*}: = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}{V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}\quad(2)$$

where $V_{\text{Cox}}\left( {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)$ is the estimated variance of the Cox model survival estimate for the new patient at time $t$. The variance of the Cox model survival estimate can be estimated through several methods. A standard estimator is based on the delta method,[@tsiatis1981; @andersen1993] which is implemented in frequently used software for survival analysis (details in Supplement 2).[@package-survival; @mstate2011] Using the delta method variance estimator, effective sample size for a Cox model prediction of a patient with covariate values $x_{\text{new}}$ at time $t$ is:

$$N_{*}\left( t,x_{\text{new}} \right) = \frac{{\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t)\left( 1 - {\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}(t) \right)}{\exp\left( 2{\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{\text{new}} \right){\widehat{S}}_{\text{new}}^{2}(t)\left\lbrack \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{i}}{\left( \sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right) \right)^{2}} + w^{\top}I\left( \widehat{\beta} \right)^{- 1}w \right\rbrack},\quad(3)$$

where $w = \left( w_{1},\ldots,w_{p} \right)$ is a vector of partial derivatives, with $w_{q}$ the partial derivative of the survival function in the direction of $\beta_{q}$ for $q \in \{ 1,\ldots,p\}$ with:

$$w_{q} = \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{i}}{\sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right)}\left( {\overline{x}}_{q} - x_{\text{new},q} \right),\quad(4)$$

with ${\overline{x}}_{q}$ the risk-weighted average of $x_{q}$ in the population (Supplement 2), and $d_{i}$ the number of events at time $t_{i}$.

Other methods exist for estimating the variance, such as the Von Mises expansion,[@vandervaart1998; @riskRegression] or the infinitesimal jackknife.[@survival-vignette] Any of these methods can be applied for estimating effective sample size using Equation (2).

### 2.2 Interpretation

The effective sample size of a Cox model survival prediction is determined by the variance of the estimated prediction, which comprises two components: the uncertainty in the estimated survival probability given the coefficients, and the uncertainty in the estimated coefficients. One difference between the Cox model and nonparametric setting is that the count of patients at risk is replaced by the sum of risk scores.[@therneau2000] In a survival setting without covariates, the Nelson-Aalen estimator for the cumulative hazard is:[@nelson1972; @aalen1978]

$$\widehat{H}(t) = \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{i}}{n_{i}},\ \ \ (5)$$

where $n_{i}$ is the number of patients at risk. Every patient at risk at time $t_{i}$ contributes exactly 1 to the denominator: $n_{i} = \sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}1$.

The cumulative baseline hazard of the Cox model is commonly estimated using the Breslow estimator:[@breslow1974]

$${\widehat{H}}_{0}(t) = \sum_{i:t_{i} \leq t}^{}\frac{d_{i}}{\sum_{j \in R_{i}}^{}\exp\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right)}.\ \ \ \ \ (6)$$

While at risk, each patient contributes a weight equal to their risk score, $\exp{\left( {\widehat{\beta}}^{\top}x_{j} \right),\ \ }$ to the denominator at all $t$, because of the proportional hazards assumption. While the Nelson-Aalen estimator of the cumulative hazard is an aggregate over time, its hazard increments $(\Delta\widehat{H}\left( t_{i} \right) = \ \frac{d_{i}}{n_{i}})$ are purely local, relying only on the count of individuals at risk at a specific time $t_{i}$. In contrast, the estimated hazard increments from the Breslow estimator utilize the estimated coefficients $\widehat{\beta}$ which are derived from the entire follow-up period.

Because $\widehat{\beta}$ is estimated using all events across the entire follow-up period, the model effectively uses information of events that occur after $t_{i}$ to estimate the baseline hazard estimate at $t_{i}$. For many patients, specifically those with risk scores close to or below the risk-weighted mean of the population, this global estimation of $\widehat{\beta}$ results in a lower prediction variance than the local counting process used in the Nelson-Aalen estimator (Supplement 3).

In addition, there is variance in the estimated coefficients, $V\left( \widehat{\beta} \right) = \ I\left( \widehat{\beta} \right)^{- 1}$. This variance is linked to the survival estimate through the gradient of the survival function with respect to the coefficients, captured in $w$ (Equation (4)). This gradient depends on the distance between a patient's covariates $x$ and the risk-weighted mean of the covariates. For patients with exceptional covariate profiles far from the population mean, the gradient is larger, which increases variance and reduces $N_{*}$. This risk-weighted mean reflects the composition of the risk set $R(t)$ at time $t$. The risk set evolves over time as patients experience the event or are censored and the risk-weighted mean changes with it. The exceptionality of a patient profile is therefore time-dependent.

### 2.3 Software

All analyses were conducted in R,[@R] version 4.5.1, using the packages survival[@package-survival] and mstate.[@mstate2011] Simulations were run using the simsurv package.[@package-simsurv] Code used for this article, including functions that can calculate the effective sample size for a `survfit.coxph` object in R can be found on GitHub: <https://github.com/survival-lumc/EffectiveSampleSize_Cox>. All $N_{*}$ estimates are based on coxph, which handles ties with Efron's method.

## 3 Application to real data

### 3.1 Data description

We performed analyses in the colon dataset as available within the survival package[@package-survival] in R. This data set contains colorectal cancer patients who underwent a curative resection and were enrolled in a randomized controlled trial. Treatment arms were adjuvant levamisole ('Lev'); levamisole+5-fluorouracil ('Lev+5FU'); or untreated as a control arm ('Obs').[@laurie1989; @moertel1995] Overall survival was the primary outcome for 929 patients. Four baseline prognostic factors were considered in this study: treatment as randomized ('rx', 3 categories); tumor adherence to adjacent organs ('adhere', 2 categories); age ('age', continuous); and number of positive lymph nodes ('nodes', continuous, Supplement 4). The data example is used for illustration purposes only.

Second, we investigated effective sample size of predictions in multiple real-world datasets. Cox models were fitted on 8 datasets that are available within the survival package.[@package-survival] The datasets are: the aforementioned colon cancer data (colon)[@laurie1989; @moertel1995]; a randomized trial in primary biliary cholangitis (pbc); the Veterans' Administration lung cancer trial (veteran); the North Central Cancer Treatment Group cohort of patients with advanced lung cancer (lung); the Rotterdam tumor bank cohort (rotterdam)[@royston2013]; the German Breast Cancer Study Group trial (gbsg)[@royston2013]; a population-based cohort with serum free light chain measurements (flchain); and a cohort of patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (mgus2). The datasets differ in sample size (137 to 6,521 patients) and event rate (30% to 93%). Overall survival was the outcome of interest in all datasets except gbsg, which only contains recurrence-free survival. In pbc, liver transplantation was treated as censoring.

### 3.2 Illustration with one predictor

We compared Cox models with a single categorical predictor to Kaplan-Meier curves for the two categorical variables 'rx' and 'adhere'. At early time points, the Cox model yielded substantially higher effective sample sizes than the stratified Kaplan-Meier curves. Remarkably, the effective sample size for the Cox model predictions exceeded the total development sample size for early survival estimates in the Lev+5FU treatment arm and the "no adherence" group. This unintuitive surplus ($N_{*} > N$) decreased as events accumulated over the follow-up period (Figure 1). The higher effective sample size for the Cox model predictions corresponded with narrower confidence intervals compared to Kaplan-Meier estimates, particularly early in follow-up (Supplement 5).

Next, we illustrate the properties of $N_{*}$ using a single continuous covariate. For patients of median age, the effective sample size remained close to the total population size until the onset of censoring (Figure 2). For those at the 75th or 99th percentiles, the estimated effective sample size initially decreased and remained stable until six years of follow-up, in line with censoring occurring mainly after six years. While survival predictions were similar for all three example patients due to the minor prognostic impact of age (HR 1.02 \[95% CI 0.93 -- 1.13\] per SD increase), the uncertainty was notably larger for those with rare age profiles. We observed a similar phenomenon for the number of nodes. Patients with the median value (2 nodes) had $N_{*} > N$. For a patient with 17 nodes, the effective sample size increased slightly over time with the survival probability approaching zero (Figure 2).

### 3.3 Effective sample size in multivariable Cox models

Cox model predictions are typically based on multiple predictors and presented as survival probabilities at specific time points. We fit four sequential models and make 5-year survival predictions for all patients in the development data to investigate the impact of increasing complexity: (A) treatment; (B) treatment and tumor adherence; (C) treatment, adherence, and number of positive nodes; and (D) treatment, adherence, nodes, and age (Figure 3). With each additional predictor, the median effective sample size ($N_{*}$) in the development population decreased: 337 for model A, 329 for model B, 325 for model C, and 253 for model D. At 5 years, 89% of the observed events had occurred and $N_{*}$ was below $N$ for all patients.

The addition of adherence to a model based only on treatment changed the predicted probabilities and substantially reduced $N_{*}$ for the smaller category of patients with tumor adherence, though its impact on median $N_{*}$ was small. Similarly, the number of nodes decreased $N_{*}$ for many patients while increasing the spread in predictions, yet the median $N_{*}$ remained relatively stable. In contrast, the inclusion of age resulted in only a minor increase in the spread of predictions while introducing substantial heterogeneity in $N_{*}$ and a large decrease in median $N_{*}$. Indeed, age was a weak predictor (delta Cox-Snell $R^{2}\ 0.15\%$) of the survival outcome, whereas the number of nodes was a much stronger predictor (delta Cox-Snell $R^{2}\ 7.7\%$).

### 3.4 Effective sample size in multiple models

While $N_{*}$ can exceed $N$ early on in follow-up, this was not observed in the single real-data example in Figure 3. To consider what happens in a broader set of possible real-data prediction models at various time horizons, we checked Cox models developed on the complete cases in 8 datasets. All variables in the data are considered, with the final model based on backward selection of the variables. Prediction time horizons were unified by taking them at times $t$ when a specific fraction ($f \in \{ 0.01,\ 0.1,\ 0.25,\ 0.4,\ 0.6,\ 0.75,\ 0.9\}$) of the total events in the data have occurred. We compared the distribution of $N_{*}$ of patients in the data to the development sample size $N$.

For most models, $N_{*}$ drops below $N$ for most of the patients from the time when 25-40% of the total events have been observed (Figure 4). Harrell's C seems related to the frequency that $N_{*} > N$ occurs.


## 4 Investigation of effective sample size in simulations

### 4.1 Simulation setting

We conducted two simulation studies to evaluate the behavior of effective sample size ($N_{*}$).

The first simulation study investigated $N_{*}$ early on in follow-up in a large dataset ($N = 10,000$) without censoring. We simulated a constant baseline hazard ($h_{0}(t) = 1$) and considered a single predictor: either a binary indicator $X_{1}$ (with exactly half the population assigned $X_{1} = 1$) or a continuous variable $X_{2} \sim N(0,1)$. In both scenarios, the hazard ratio (HR) was set to $2$.

The second simulation study investigated where $N_{*}$ exceeds $N$. Additionally, it also checks the coverage of the 95% confidence intervals for predictions based on a given $N_{*}$. A full description of the simulation study according to the ADEMP framework can be found in Supplement 7.[@morris2019] Follow-up ended at a common end-time $\tau$. We varied the true marginal probability of an event by time $\tau$, $1\  - \ S(\tau)$ (hereafter "event rate"), where $S(\tau)$ is the survival probability at $\tau$ averaged over the covariate distribution of the population. We simulate datasets with the event rate at time $\tau$ set to $1 - S(\tau) \in \{ 0.01,\ 0.05,\ 0.1,\ 0.3,\ 0.6,\ 0.9,\ 0.99\}$ and sample size $N = \frac{500}{1 - S(\tau)}$ so that the expected number of events without censoring is always 500. We simulate follow-up without censoring, or uniform censoring over the interval $\lbrack 0.2\tau,\tau\rbrack$ to emulate common registry inclusion mechanisms. Event times followed a Weibull distribution with three binary $Bern(0.5)$ and three continuous $N(0,1)$ variables with equal contributions to the linear predictor, scaled to a specified c-statistic $(c = 0.8)$ for the resulting Cox model. All scenarios were run with 1000 replications. The estimands were the survival probabilities and effective sample sizes of 200 covariate profiles, chosen at equally spaced quantiles of the true linear predictor, at seven time points when 5%, 10%, 25%, 40%, 60%, 75% and 90% of all events in the data had been observed. We report the percentage of predictions with $N_{*} > N$, among all predictions with the same survival $S(t|\mathbf{x})$. Second, we report the coverage of the 95% log(-log) confidence interval, as functions of the true survival probability pooled over the time points. The number of predictors, noise predictors, the Weibull shape, c-statistics and additional independent censoring were varied in sensitivity analyses (Supplement 7).

Detailed technical specifications and the code required for full reproducibility are provided in the Supplementary Materials and on Github: <https://github.com/survival-lumc/EffectiveSampleSize_Cox>.

### 4.2 Behavior early in follow-up

In the first simulation study, Cox model-based survival estimates yielded higher effective sample sizes than the actual number of patients in each group. For the binary predictor, $N_{*}$ started at $15,000$ for the low-risk group ($X_{1} = 0$) and $7,500$ for the high-risk group ($X_{1} = 1$), despite both groups containing exactly $5,000$ patients (Figure 5B).

Decomposing the variance revealed that this high $N_{*}$ was driven almost entirely by the variance attributable to the baseline hazard estimation early in follow-up (Figure 5C). Because the Cox model utilizes global information from all events to estimate the baseline hazard, it provided a more precise estimate than the local Kaplan-Meier approach.

For the continuous predictor $X_{2}$, $N_{*}$ exhibited significant heterogeneity; while patients at the mean ($X_{2} = 0$) initially had an $N_{*}$ above the total population size, those with above average risk scores ($X_{2} = 1$) had a rapid decrease in $N_{*}$ over time with their survival probability decreasing (Figure 5E).

Notably, equally unique patients, such as those with $X_{2} = 1$ and $X_{2} = - 1$, did not share the same effective sample size. This asymmetry occurred because their different survival probabilities and different gradients with respect to the coefficient over time resulted in distinct $N_{*}$ trajectories. Specifically, as follow-up progressed, the relative impact of coefficient uncertainty evolved differently for high-risk versus low-risk profiles. High-risk individuals are more likely to experience the event and leave the risk set. This further separates their effective sample sizes despite their equal distance from the population mean at time 0.


### 4.3 Effective sample size based on survival probability

The second simulation study showed that $N_{*} > N$ occurred exclusively at high and low survival probabilities. The survival probability above which $N_{*} > N$ depends mostly on the event rate in the data (Figure 6). We observed that \>5% predictions have $N_{*} > N$ above $S \approx 0.90$ for a 99% event rate; above $S \approx 0.95$ at a 30% event rate; and above $S \approx 0.99$ at a 10% event rate. Harrell's C had little influence on these thresholds, but changes the number of patients with more extreme survival probabilities (Supplement 7). Censoring lowers the number of observed events and increases the survival probability threshold where $N_{*} > N$ occurs.

The coverage of the 95% log(-log) confidence intervals, based on the model-based variance of the Cox model (with Efron's method for ties), was close to 95% for all effective sample sizes (Figure 7). Even at extreme values of $N_{*}/N$, the coverage was good. This indicates that extreme effective sample sizes reflect genuinely small variances.


## 5 Discussion

This study shows that effective sample size behaves in a complicated way for the Cox proportional hazards model. We relate our findings to the desired properties mentioned in the introduction.

1.  Intuitive behavior: effective sample size decreases as events and censoring accumulate, in line with the Kaplan-Meier effective sample size (Figure 1). However, $N_{*}$ can, and likely will, exceed the total sample size $N$ at high and low survival probabilities. This is a property of the model. High effective sample size ($N_{*} > N$) reflects genuinely low variance (Figure 7). When using $N_{*}$ for communication, $N_{*} > N$ can still be considered problematic. In that case, $N_{*}$ should only be used when the survival probabilities drop below the thresholds shown in Figure 6.

2.  Reflection of exceptionality: Effective sample size reflects the commonality of a patient profile within the development data. This desired property is met as shown in Figure 3. Patients with common profiles, such as the median age, have an effective sample size similar to the total sample size in the absence of censoring, while patients with exceptional covariate values have a low effective sample size. This behavior was not symmetric however, as patients with similar exceptionality (covariate value of 1 SD from the mean value) had quite different effective sample sizes due to different survival probabilities (Figure 5).

### 5.1 Efficiency of the Cox model

Effective sample sizes larger than the development sample size are not exclusive to the Cox model, they have also been described in logistic regression for extreme probabilities.[@thomassen2024] For the Cox model, $N_{*} > N$ appears more frequently, especially at high survival probabilities. This observation may reflect the model's informational efficiency relative to the binomial distribution used as a reference for the variance of $S(t)$.

A driving force of this efficiency is the proportional hazards assumption, which allows for the global estimation of coefficients ($\beta$) over the entire follow-up period.[@cox1972; @efron1977] Calculating $N_{*}$ involves equating the Cox model prediction variance with binomial sampling variance. This comparison implicitly suggests one could achieve the same precision as the model by conducting a binomial experiment on $N_{*}$ clones of the patient. Because the binomial experiment relies on the outcome at a single point in time, it is less efficient than the Cox model, which extracts more information from the data by using the timing of all events. Comparisons of the Cox model to logistic regression demonstrate this increased efficiency (Supplement 10).[@green1983; @annesi1989] Cox model predictions yield narrower confidence intervals than logistic regression predictions, but maintain nominal 95% coverage if the model is well-specified (Figure 7, Supplement 7, 10). If the proportional hazards assumption is violated, the model predictions may have narrow confidence intervals while the prediction is biased.

### 5.2 Effective sample size in model development

The addition of covariates to a Cox model had different impacts on the spread of predictions and their corresponding effective sample sizes (Figure 3). This illustrates that a balance must be struck between bias and variance when making individual predictions. For example, the addition of age to the model resulted in only minor changes to predicted probabilities yet substantially decreased $N_{*}$ for older and younger patients. During development, such trade-offs must be considered.

Recent sample size guidelines focus on reliable estimation of the average risk and limiting overfitting. For instance, a minimum of 100 patients may be recommended to estimate an overall event rate with a 20% relative uncertainty of ±0.1.[@steyerbergbook; @harrellblog; @steyerberg2026] Furthermore, managing model complexity has historically relied on rules of thumb, such as 10 to 15 events per variable (EPV) for proportional hazards regression.[@peduzzi1995; @harrellbook] These general rules have faced criticism[@vansmeden2016; @riley2019] and primarily ensure that the model is well-specified on average.

As a diagnostic tool, $N_{*}$ provides an individualized complement to these global metrics. As exemplified in Figure 3, specific individuals can exhibit very low effective sample sizes even while the median effective sample size is adequate. This allows developers to identify covariate profiles where predictions are deemed too uncertain for clinical decision-making. To mitigate these risks, modelers might consider winsorizing continuous covariate values[@royston2000; @aguinis2013] or implementing penalized prediction methods to stabilize estimates in the tails of the predictor distributions.[@houwelingen1990; @verweij1994]

Guidelines for acceptable effective sample size are inherently context dependent. However, we suggest that in addition to meeting global sample size requirements, modelers should aim for a median $N_{*}$ of at least 100 to ensure adequate certainty for most of the population.[@harrellblog] Additionally, $N_{*}$ of at least 10 might be a minimum for any individual covariate profile.[@thomassen2024]

### 5.3 Communication of effective sample size

Effective sample size intends to be an interpretable metric for communicating uncertainty in clinical predictions. For linear models, generalized linear models, machine learning, and Kaplan-Meier estimates, the measure may serve as an intuitive supplement to, or replacement for, standard 95% confidence intervals.[@thomassen2024; @thomassen2025; @hackmann2025] Extending this metric to the Cox model appears to be more nuanced.

Communication of model results is especially important for shared decision-making for preference-sensitive clinical decisions.[@stiggelbout2015] Implementing this collaborative process requires decision support tools such as prognostic models.[@4Dpicture] These models carry inherent uncertainty that may need to be communicated for a fair informed deliberation.[@4Dpicture; @pieterse2026] Communicating such uncertainty may undermine trust to some extent, even if the impact is small.[@fischhoff2012; @vanderbles2020] Transparency is particularly relevant when risks are framed using frequency statements, such as: "If we had 100 patients like you, we would expect X to survive".[@kattan2002] In this context, $N_{*}$ can be used to qualify the denominator, specifying that the estimate is not based on an arbitrary 100 individuals, but effectively on $N_{*}$ patients. This approach combines risk communication with an estimate of uncertainty. Future research is needed to determine a preferable format for clinical communication.

Using $N_{*}$ for direct communication with patients requires a choice on how to deal with $N_{*} > N$. High $N_{*}$ could be considered a reflection of high prediction certainty and reported as is. A prediction 'based on 2000 patients like you', even if the development sample size was 1000, means that we are as certain of the predicted outcome as we would be in a binomial experiment based on 2000 patients. This surplus $N_{*} > N$ is attributable to modelling assumptions. Alternatively, $N_{*} > N$ could be considered misleading in communication with patients. In this case we recommend using $N_{*}$ only for predictions with survival probabilities where $N_{*} > N$ typically does not occur. In general this is for survival probabilities $0.01 < S\left( t \middle| x \right) < 0.9$. In situations with lower event rates, $N_{*}$ can be used for predictions of $S\left( t \middle| x \right) < 0.95$ (event rate of 30%) or even $S\left( t \middle| x \right) < 0.99$ (event rate of 10%) as upper bound.

### 5.4 Effective sample size for other survival models

In general, effective sample size is simply a ratio of the binomial variance of the predicted survival probability, to the variance of the prediction. In this article, we have used closed-form variance estimators, but variance can also be estimated through other methods. For more complex survival models, such as random survival forests or penalized regression models like LASSO Cox, the variance can also be computed using the (parametric) bootstrap.[@thomassen2025] For Cox models, bootstrapped effective sample sizes differ slightly from model-based methods. The parametric bootstrap seems to outperform the nonparametric bootstrap, which consistently estimates lower $N_{*}$ compared to model-based methods (Supplement 11).

Effective sample size could also be applied to competing risks and multi-state models. The definition itself carries over to any predicted probability for which a variance can be estimated, for example with the delta method or the bootstrap. However, these settings present additional challenges, such as which predicted quantity is most suitable for effective sample size, and they require further research.

## 6 Conclusion

Effective sample size ($N_{*}$) for the Cox model is a complex measure for quantifying the uncertainty of individual survival predictions. By incorporating both event status and timing, the Cox model leverages more information from the patient timeline than the discrete binomial experiment underlying the $N_{*}$ metric.[@efron1977; @green1983] Unlike the Kaplan-Meier setting, where $N_{*}$ is constrained by the sample size of a specific stratum,[@hackmann2025] $N_{*}$ for Cox models typically exceeds $N$ at high and low survival probabilities.

While $N_{*} > N$ follows directly from the statistical properties of the estimator and reflects genuine low uncertainty, it may be difficult to interpret in risk communication. To avoid communicating $N_{*} > N$, we recommend only using effective sample size to communicate prediction uncertainty for survival predictions between 1% and 90%. For models in settings with low event rates, this upper bound could be higher than 90%. Future research should evaluate the impact of $N_{*}$ on patient perception of uncertainty in risk communication and its utility in guiding model development decisions.
